pathophysiology.summary: Anaphylaxis is a serious, rapid-onset systemic hypersensitivity reaction that compromises the airway, breathing and/or circulation. Mast cell and basophil mediators cause airway oedema, bronchospasm, vasodilation, capillary leak and sometimes myocardial depression.
keyMechanisms: Airway and breathing: tissue oedema and smooth-muscle contraction cause laryngeal swelling, bronchospasm and wheeze (commonest in food-induced anaphylaxis).

Circulation: vasodilation plus capillary leak causes distributive and hypovolaemic shock; up to 35% of blood volume can leak out within 10 minutes. Myocardial depression and ischaemic ECG changes can occur even with normal coronaries.
Posture: sitting or standing a hypotensive patient reduces venous return and has caused cardiovascular collapse and death; keep them supine (or semi-recumbent if breathless).

Why adrenaline works: alpha effects reverse vasodilation and oedema; beta effects open the airways, increase myocardial contraction and suppress mast-cell mediator release. Delay is linked to protracted and fatal reactions.
Biphasic reactions (about 5%): symptoms recur hours later without re-exposure; median time about 12 h.

symptoms: Sudden onset over minutes after a trigger (drug, food, insect sting, contrast, vaccine). Parenteral triggers act fastest.
Breathing difficulty, throat tightness, hoarseness; dizziness or collapse.
Abdominal cramps, vomiting, incontinence; anxiety or 'sense of impending doom'.
Skin and mucosal changes (flushing, urticaria, angioedema) in over 80%, but absent in up to 20%.
physicalSigns: Airway: lip, tongue or throat swelling, hoarseness, stridor.
Breathing: tachypnoea, wheeze, fatigue, cyanosis, SpO2 below 92%, confusion.
Circulation: pale, clammy, hypotension, tachycardia (bradycardia is a late, pre-arrest sign), drowsiness or coma.
redFlags: Stridor, hoarseness or tongue swelling: impending airway obstruction; most experienced person to intubate early
No improvement after two doses of IM adrenaline: refractory anaphylaxis; call critical care and start an IV adrenaline infusion
Patient on a beta-blocker with poor response: give glucagon
Never sit or stand a hypotensive patient up
precipitants: Drugs (antibiotics, NSAIDs, contrast, anaesthetic agents), blood products, vaccines.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Wheeze without skin, circulatory or allergen features; anaphylaxis can look identical (especially in children). If in doubt, give IM adrenaline.
Swelling of lips, tongue or airway without urticaria in a patient on an ACE inhibitor; usually does not respond to adrenaline.
Throat tightness and stridor without objective allergic features; does not respond to adrenaline.
Bradycardia, pallor, quick recovery when lying flat; no urticaria, wheeze or angioedema.
Hyperventilation, tingling; no hypotension, hypoxia, wheeze or rash. Can be hard to separate in people with previous anaphylaxis.
Skin or mucosal changes only, without airway, breathing or circulation problems: not anaphylaxis.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Sudden airway and/or breathing and/or circulation problem, usually with skin changes.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Diagnosis is clinical. Treat immediately; never wait for tests.

references.title: Saudi MoH Protocol for Adult and Pediatric Management of Anaphylaxis

clinicalManagement.title: Rapid ABCDE Assessment & Call for Help
actions: Airway: Check for swelling of the tongue, lips or throat, hoarseness and stridor; keep the airway open and call for expert airway help early if obstruction is impending.

Breathing: Check respiratory rate, wheeze and cyanosis; if SpO2 is below 94% give [💊 Oxygen | 15 L/min via reservoir mask | Inhaled | Continuous | Until SpO2 94–98%, then titrate to target] (MOH: 8–10 L/min by face mask, up to 100%).
Circulation: Check for pallor, clammy skin, tachycardia and hypotension; secure IV or IO access; fluids follow in the Circulation step.

Disability: Assess alert, voice, pain, unresponsive (AVPU) and confusion; check pupils and capillary glucose; if glucose is below 4 mmol/L give [💊 Glucose 10% | 150–200 mL | IV infusion over 15 minutes | Repeat once after 10 minutes if glucose remains below 4 mmol/L | Until glucose 4 mmol/L or above].
Exposure: Check skin and mucosa for urticaria, flushing and angioedema while keeping the patient warm.
Correct each abnormality concurrently as it is found: do not wait for the full survey or a confirmed diagnosis before treating, and call for help (resuscitation team) early.

Use World Allergy Organization (WAO) criteria; if in doubt, give [💊 Adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000) | 0.5 mg (0.5 mL), adults and children over 12 years | IM, anterolateral mid-thigh | Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement | Until airway, breathing and circulation problems resolve] immediately. Remove the trigger (stop the suspected drug, infusion or colloid; remove the sting).
Positioning: Lie flat with legs raised; sit up only if breathing is easier; left side if pregnant; avoid sudden standing.

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate Pharmacological Intervention
actions: First-line treatment, given before any other drug (RCUK 2021; MOH range 0.3–0.5 mg): [💊 Adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000) | 0.5 mg (0.5 mL), adults and children over 12 years | IM, anterolateral mid-thigh | Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement | Until airway, breathing and circulation problems resolve].

Children (RCUK 2021): [💊 Adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000) | 0.3 mg (0.3 mL), children 6–12 years | IM, anterolateral mid-thigh | Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement | Until airway, breathing and circulation problems resolve]; [💊 Adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000) | 0.15 mg (0.15 mL), children 6 months to 6 years | IM, anterolateral mid-thigh | Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement | Until airway, breathing and circulation problems resolve]; [💊 Adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000) | 0.1–0.15 mg (0.1–0.15 mL), infants under 6 months | IM, anterolateral mid-thigh | Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement | Until airway, breathing and circulation problems resolve].

If airway, breathing or circulation problems persist, repeat the dose after 5 minutes (MOH: every 5–15 minutes as needed): [💊 Adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000) | 0.5 mg (0.5 mL), adults and children over 12 years | IM, anterolateral mid-thigh | Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement | Until airway, breathing and circulation problems resolve].
Immediate intubation by the most experienced available operator.

clinicalManagement.title: Circulation
actions: Fluids (adults): [💊 Sodium chloride 0.9% (crystalloid) | 500–1000 mL, up to 1–2 L in severe shock | IV or IO bolus, rapidly | Repeat as needed | Until blood pressure is restored].

Fluids (children): [💊 Sodium chloride 0.9% (crystalloid) | 10 mL/kg, up to 20 mL/kg rapidly for hypotension | IV or IO bolus | Repeat, to a maximum of 50 mL/kg in the first 30 minutes | Until blood pressure is restored] (ASCIA 2024).
Give fluids early in refractory anaphylaxis (RCUK 2021).
Use IO access if IV access is delayed.

clinicalManagement.title: Refractory Anaphylaxis
actions: Seek expert help early; start an infusion only in a specialist setting by skilled clinicians (RCUK 2021): [💊 Adrenaline infusion | 1 mg in 100 mL 0.9% sodium chloride at 0.5 mL/kg/h (about 0.1 microgram/kg/min); 1 mL/kg/h if hypotensive or hypoxic | IV via a dedicated peripheral line, or IO | Continuous; titrate every 5–10 minutes to the lowest effective rate | Wean 1 hour after full resolution over 30 minutes, then stop]. MOH: start at 0.1 microgram/kg/min and titrate.

Continue IM dosing every 5 minutes until an infusion is running: [💊 Adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000) | 0.5 mg (0.5 mL), adults and children over 12 years | IM, anterolateral mid-thigh | Every 5 minutes until an infusion is running | Until the infusion is running].

Beta-blocker patients may need a rescue drug for refractory shock (discuss with a specialist) (ASCIA 2024): [💊 Glucagon | 1 mg (RCUK) or 1–5 mg over 5 minutes then 5–15 microgram/min (MOH) | IV | Repeat 1 mg if no response, or infusion 1–2 mg/h (RCUK) | Until response].
Persistent upper-airway obstruction: [💊 Adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000), nebulised | 5 mL | Nebulised | Repeat as needed, may be given despite an infusion | Until stridor settles] (ASCIA 2024).

Persistent wheeze: [💊 Salbutamol | 8–12 puffs of 100 micrograms | Inhaled via spacer | Repeat as needed | Until wheeze resolves] or [💊 Salbutamol | 5 mg | Nebulised | Repeat as needed | Until wheeze resolves]; the inhaled bronchodilator does not treat upper-airway obstruction or shock (ASCIA 2024).

If still refractory, critical care adds one vasopressor by expert titration: [💊 Noradrenaline | 0.05–0.5 microgram/kg/min | IV infusion via central line | Continuous, titrated to blood pressure | Until haemodynamically stable]; alternatives are [💊 Dopamine | 5–20 microgram/kg/min | IV infusion | Continuous, titrated to blood pressure | Until haemodynamically stable] (MOH) or [💊 Vasopressin | 0.01–0.04 units/min | IV infusion | Continuous, titrated to blood pressure | Until haemodynamically stable] (RCUK).
Start cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and follow advanced life support protocols immediately.
Give [💊 Atropine | 0.5 mg | IV | Repeat if necessary | Until the heart rate recovers, maximum 3 mg] (RCUK).

clinicalManagement.title: After Stabilisation
actions: Do not stand or walk the patient until haemodynamically stable: usually at least 1 hour after one dose of [💊 Adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000) | 0.5 mg (0.5 mL), adults and children over 12 years | IM, anterolateral mid-thigh | Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement | Until airway, breathing and circulation problems resolve], or 4 hours after more than one dose (ASCIA 2024).

Observe in hospital for at least 4 hours after the last dose of [💊 Adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000) | 0.5 mg (0.5 mL), adults and children over 12 years | IM, anterolateral mid-thigh | Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement | Until airway, breathing and circulation problems resolve]. Overnight observation is strongly recommended for severe or protracted cases, concomitant illness, living alone or remote, or late-evening presentations (ASCIA 2024).

RCUK 2021 observation: fast-track discharge after 2 hours from resolution only with a good response within 5–10 minutes to a single dose given within 30 minutes of onset, complete resolution, trained-in-use auto-injectors and adequate supervision; at least 6 hours after resolution if 2 IM doses were needed or there was a previous biphasic reaction; at least 12 hours if more than 2 doses were needed, severe asthma or severe respiratory compromise, possible continuing absorption, late-night presentation or poor access to emergency care. MOH: observe 6 hours if airway compromise, repeated IM doses, coronary artery disease, asthma, or on beta-blockers or ACE inhibitors.

Third-line medication for persistent skin symptoms: a non-sedating oral antihistamine such as [💊 Cetirizine | 10 mg | Oral (MOH: IV over 2 minutes) | Once | Single dose]; MOH also lists [💊 Diphenhydramine | 25–50 mg | IV | Once | Single dose] and [💊 Famotidine | 20 mg | IV | Once | Single dose].

Corticosteroids are not routine (RCUK 2021); for refractory reactions or coexisting asthma consider [💊 Hydrocortisone | 200 mg | IV | Once | Single dose]; MOH lists [💊 Methylprednisolone | 125 mg | IV | Once | Single dose].

Discharge: Refer every patient to an allergy clinic and prescribe [💊 Adrenaline auto-injector | 300 micrograms (150 micrograms for children 7.5–20 kg) | IM, anterolateral mid-thigh | Once, repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement and a second device is available | Single dose per episode] with training and an action plan, unless the reaction was drug-induced (RCUK 2021; ASCIA 2024).

learningObjectives: Recognise, investigate and manage acute anaphylaxis in the emergency department.
pitfalls: Giving antihistamine or steroid first and delaying adrenaline.
IV bolus adrenaline outside cardiac arrest.
Missing anaphylaxis without a rash (absent in up to 20%).
Discharging early without a risk-based observation period or auto-injector.
keyPoints: If in doubt, give IM adrenaline 0.5 mg into the thigh.
Repeat after 5 minutes if not better; after two doses, start an IV adrenaline infusion.
Lie the patient flat; never stand a hypotensive patient up.
Antihistamines and steroids do not treat airway, breathing or circulation problems.
Tryptase at 1–2 h, refer to allergy, auto-injector on discharge.
